p1.title:
A prompt isn't a question.
It's a work order.
p1.desc: Chapter 3 was the one we rewrote most while making Awesome AI Bible 2026. Role, context, task, format, constraint — write all five down and the same result comes back the next time. That is the difference between a hobby and work.

p2.title:
Why the ninja cat
fails every time
p2.desc: Kuro is the clumsiest ninja cat in the village. Every mission goes wrong, and it goes wrong in exactly the way a child hopes it will. A picture book for ages 4–8, published in Korean and Japanese together.

p3.title:
Learning to start a business
in a kingdom with no prices
p3.desc: An Introduction to ISEKAI Entrepreneurship teaches business without a textbook in sight. A founder lands in a kingdom that has never heard of a fixed price and builds its markets one at a time.

bio.akira-murata:
Born in Kamakura. He spent several years in Brighton and now lives in Chiba — all three of them places within sight of the sea.

He decides what Awesome Books Asia publishes. He teaches economics at a university and, separately, works on AI with government ministries and universities across ASEAN; he does not regard the three as different jobs. "Economics and AI ask the same question in different ways — how does a person decide?" It is why Quantum Economics, Awesome AI Bible 2026 and AIの答えに、人間は何を足すのか sit under one name, and why this house published all three.

He keeps a notebook of questions he could not answer. Lecture room or ministry meeting room, whatever went unanswered in the moment goes into it. The books mostly come out of that notebook.

AIの答えに、人間は何を足すのか did. At a ministry workshop somewhere in ASEAN, a civil servant asked him: "The AI has given us an answer. Can we put it forward as policy as it stands?" He had nothing to say that day. The book is the late reply.

He translates from English into Japanese. None of his translations has been published yet; one is in preparation.
bio.lyra-mizuki:
Born in Hilo, Hawai'i. Her father ran a flower nursery; her mother kept the small bookshop next door. She grew up between Japanese and English and says neither ever felt entirely hers. She moved to Tokyo at twenty-six.

She lives in Shimokitazawa — narrow lanes, second-hand clothes shops and small theatres. "Nobody here has to explain what they do," is the reason she gives. She does not write at home: the manuscript gets written at a corner table in a kissaten that has not moved in twenty years.

She writes fantasy, but what interests her is economics. "The interesting thing about another world isn't the magic," she says. "It's who sets the prices." An Introduction to ISEKAI Entrepreneurship began as notes to a friend who was starting a business. The first draft was forty-two letters.
bio.fumi-yamaneko:
Born and still living in Yanaka, Tokyo — a district the war and the earthquake both missed, so the wooden houses, the temples and the cats are all still there. Yamaneko, mountain cat, was a nickname her kindergarten class gave her. Given the neighbourhood, nobody found it odd.

She taught kindergarten for twelve years before her first book. She writes for children who are bad at the thing everyone else finds easy. Kuro fails at hiding, which for a ninja is the whole job. "There are already far too many stories about fixing what you're bad at," she says.

She thumbnails on the backs of receipts. Her editor has two boxes of them.
bio.orion-carter:
Born in Bristol, moved to Byron Bay at six. He left art school after two years and made a living painting signs and surf-shop murals.

He has no studio. Whatever kitchen table he is sitting at is the studio. Where he can, he draws in one continuous line without lifting the pen.

His first commission came when Fumi Yamaneko asked him for "a cat that looks like it is about to fall over". He sent twenty-three drawings. The one she chose was the second.
bio.vega-choi:
Born in Nottingham. Korean at home with her mother, Japanese at her father's dinner table, English everywhere else. She says she learned early that the same sentence runs at a different temperature in each.

She still lives in Nottingham — Trivett Square, in the Lace Market, in a flat carved out of a warehouse where lace was once stacked. The windows are twice her height, so the winters are cold, and anyone crossing the cobbles below can be heard from upstairs. "A neighbourhood of things that were brought here," she calls it. The lace, and her.

She translates from Japanese into Korean and into English — carrying her father's language into her mother's and into the one she went to school in, as she puts it. She keeps a notebook of words that will not go across easily; it is past three hundred. "A translator's work isn't carrying things over," she says. "It's choosing what to give up."
bio.joey-kim:
Born in Seoul. He lived in Nottingham and Colchester, and is back in Seoul now.

Before Awesome Books Asia he worked connecting Israeli companies with Korea. As a job that meant standing between two places that did not speak each other's language, which is not so far from this one.

He has two children. That they should learn from books, and that what will still matter when AI has changed everything is their education — that is the whole reason a publisher does the writing and the translating himself when he does not have to. "If I wouldn't give it to my own child, I can't publish it for someone else's."

Getting started takes him a long time, he says. Once he sits down he does not get up until it is finished. Coffee, a film or music left running, three monitors. When that is in place the day goes all at once.

He is writing Introduction to Cricket and Introduction to Rugby. He is also preparing to translate Akira Murata's books from English into Korean.
bio.halley-brooks:
Born in Sacramento. Her father moved for work and she moved with him, three high schools in all, and she says she did not speak to anyone for the first two months at any of them.

She taught English for eleven years at a public high school on the North Shore of O'ahu. She ran the music room as well, because nobody else wanted it. In that room a student who had arrived two months ago sat next to one whose family had been on that stretch of coast for three generations.

The band in North Shore is not invented, she says. "I changed the names. Everything else is as it was. How those kids learned each other's songs is not something I could have made up."

She still lives in Hale'iwa. She does not write at home; she writes in the music room after school, because that is where the piano is. The custodian comes to turn the lights off at half past five, and that is the working day.
